about: Hand-checked details for the source library. sources.json is the raw text of the workbook and is overwritten by `npm run sources`. This file is never overwritten. `overrides` fixes a workbook row (matched by id). `added` holds sources that are in the literature review or research plan but not in the workbook. `exclude` and `unconfirmed` keep a row off the site. In APA entries, *stars* mark italics.

kirkup-1993.title: From flint to stainless steel: Observations on surgical instrument composition
summary: Traces what surgical tools have been made of, from the Stone Age (flint) to the modern age (disposable plastics).
Argues the first instruments were substitutes for hands and teeth, made to pull out thorns and arrowheads.
Tools were mostly made from animal, plant, and mineral materials before metal became the standard.
The material used for tools has always followed whatever technology existed at the time.
Lists killing germs with heat as one of the big changes in what tools could be made of.
kirkup-1993.apa: Kirkup, J. (1993). From flint to stainless steel: Observations on surgical instrument composition. *Annals of the Royal College of Surgeons of England, 75*(5), 365–374.

best-2004.title: Ignaz Semmelweis and the birth of infection control
summary: The history of the Vienna doctor who figured out that doctors' unwashed hands were killing new mothers.
Describes how Semmelweis showed that handwashing prevents infection.
His book explained the finding, but it was poorly written and dismissed by other doctors.
He died in a public asylum.
best-2004.apa: Best, M., & Neuhauser, D. (2004). Ignaz Semmelweis and the birth of infection control. *Quality and Safety in Health Care, 13*(3), 233–234. https://doi.org/10.1136/qhc.13.3.233

institute-of-making-2017.title: Marvellous medical materials: Stainless steel - part one
summary: Explains why killing germs with heat forced a complete redesign of surgical tools.
The heat was destructive to the wood, ivory, and tortoiseshell that tools used to have.
All-metal instruments became the norm as a result.
Heat also sped up rusting, so tools were plated with nickel and chrome to counteract it.
Stainless steel gradually took over between 1913 and 1925.
institute-of-making-2017.apa: Institute of Making. (2017, November 8). *Marvellous medical materials: Stainless steel - part one*. https://www.instituteofmaking.org.uk/blog/marvellous-medical-material-stainless-steel-part-one

knoss-2016.title: Origins: 3D printing
summary: Tells the story of the night in 1983 when Hull printed the first object ever made with 3D printing.
The first object was a small plastic cup. His wife's reaction was disbelief.
He built the idea on nights and weekends in a borrowed lab, after more than a year of work.
He saw it as a prototyping tool, not medical technology.

farmer-2008.title: Surgery and global health: A view from beyond the OR
summary: Calls surgery in Africa the "neglected stepchild" of global public health.
Africa has fewer physicians per person than any other continent, and surgeons are even rarer.
Surgical services are almost all in cities, while most people live in rural areas.
In poor countries, surgery is mostly available to people who can pay out of pocket.
There is no Global Fund for surgery, unlike for AIDS, TB, and malaria.
farmer-2008.apa: Farmer, P. E., & Kim, J. Y. (2008). Surgery and global health: A view from beyond the OR. *World Journal of Surgery, 32*(4), 533–536. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00268-008-9525-9

ventola-2014.title: Medical applications for 3D printing: Current and projected uses
summary: A snapshot of what medical 3D printing looked like in 2014, before its popularity rose.
Sorts uses into 3 groups: making tissues and organs; making prosthetics, implants, and models; and drug research.
Explains the main printing methods used in medicine.
Shows how recently printed surgical tools became a serious idea.
ventola-2014.apa: Ventola, C. L. (2014). Medical applications for 3D printing: Current and projected uses. *P & T: A Peer-Reviewed Journal for Formulary Management, 39*(10), 704–711.

di-prima-2016.title: Additively manufactured medical products – the FDA perspective
summary: Written by FDA staff about how the FDA decides whether a printed medical product is safe to sell.
Documents the point where printed devices stopped being experimental.
Says a 3D-printed drug is already on the market.
Says the FDA's job is to allow new technology without letting unsafe products through.
di-prima-2016.apa: Di Prima, M., Coburn, J., Hwang, D., Kelly, J., Khairuzzaman, A., & Ricles, L. (2016). Additively manufactured medical products – the FDA perspective. *3D Printing in Medicine, 2*, Article 1. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41205-016-0005-9

novak-2020.title: A critical review of initial 3D printed products responding to COVID-19 health and supply chain challenges
summary: Documents what happened when hospitals ran out of supplies and people started printing replacements.
Collected data on 91 printing projects that started before April 1, 2020.
60% of the projects were protective equipment, and 62% of those were face shields.
The melted-filament method, common on hobby printers, was the most used technology.
Most projects shared designs through websites instead of official channels.
novak-2020.apa: Novak, J. I., & Loy, J. (2020). A critical review of initial 3D printed products responding to COVID-19 health and supply chain challenges. *Emerald Open Research, 2*, Article 24. https://doi.org/10.35241/emeraldopenres.13697.1

rankin-2014.title: Three-dimensional printing surgical instruments: Are we there yet?
summary: Replicated an Army-Navy retractor in PLA on an FDM (fused deposition modeling) printer. Each print took about 90 minutes.
The printed retractors withstood 13.6 kg of force before breaking.
The force was the same before and after a glutaraldehyde soak, although only one retractor was tested after the soak.
Freshly extruded PLA straight from the printer gave no PCR product when tested for traces of bacteria. The finished printed instrument did contain bacterial gene products.
Each retractor weighed 16 g and used $0.46 of PLA.
rankin-2014.apa: Rankin, T. M., Giovinco, N. A., Cucher, D. J., Watts, G., Hurwitz, B., & Armstrong, D. G. (2014). Three-dimensional printing surgical instruments: Are we there yet? *Journal of Surgical Research, 189*(2), 193–197. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jss.2014.02.020

destefano-2020.title: Applications of PLA in modern medicine
summary: Looks at PLA in tissue engineering, cardiovascular implants, dentistry, drug delivery, and orthopedics.
PLA is renewable, biodegradable, and easy to synthesize, and its properties can be changed using crystallinity and additives.
How fast PLA breaks down depends on things like its geometry, molecular weight, and crystallinity.
In lab testing, PLA blood vessel grafts slowly lost a small amount of mass but kept some structural integrity.
destefano-2020.apa: DeStefano, V., Khan, S., & Tabada, A. (2020). Applications of PLA in modern medicine. *Engineered Regeneration, 1*, 76–87. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.engreg.2020.08.002

chen-2019.title: 3D printed PLA Army-Navy retractors when used as linear retractors yield clinically acceptable tolerances
summary: Printed the same retractor model over and over while changing printer settings, then pulled on each one until it broke.
Surgeons described about 35 N as strong or clinically excessive pulling. The best printed model took more than 15 times that.
The best settings were 30% infill, 3 outer walls, a triangle pattern inside, and reinforced joints.
Spools from the same brand still made retractors with noticeably different strength.
The strongest version cost $1.25.
chen-2019.apa: Chen, J. V., Dang, A. B. C., Lee, C. S., & Dang, A. B. C. (2019). 3D printed PLA Army-Navy retractors when used as linear retractors yield clinically acceptable tolerances. *3D Printing in Medicine, 5*(1), Article 16. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41205-019-0053-z

chen-2020.title: Identifying a commercially-available 3D printing process that minimizes model distortion after annealing and autoclaving and the effect of steam sterilization on mechanical strength
summary: Printed test cubes in 7 different plastics and 4 inner patterns, and measured each one before and after heating and autoclaving.
"Annealing" means heating a printed part to make it stronger. They used a 100 °C water bath for 30 minutes.
Steam autoclaving at 134 °C ruined the strength. Untreated PLA retractors failed at 95 N, and autoclaved ones at 15.7 N.
Annealing first raised strength to 127.3 N, but autoclaving after that dropped it to 19.8 N.
Only the strength-optimized retractor design held up after both annealing and autoclaving. It failed at 164.8 N.
chen-2020.apa: Chen, J. V., Tanaka, K. S., Dang, A. B. C., & Dang, A. (2020). Identifying a commercially-available 3D printing process that minimizes model distortion after annealing and autoclaving and the effect of steam sterilization on mechanical strength. *3D Printing in Medicine, 6*(1), Article 9. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41205-020-00062-9

garnica-bohorquez-2023.title: Effect of sterilization on the dimensional and mechanical behavior of polylactic acid pieces produced by fused deposition modeling
summary: Put printed PLA through two low-cost hospital treatments in a row: formaldehyde steam, then regular steam.
Used the actual procedure from a public hospital in Bucaramanga, Colombia, instead of an idealized lab procedure.
Tested plain printed PLA test pieces, not finished instruments.
Checked whether the pieces changed shape and whether they got weaker.
Aimed at low-cost tools like surgical guides and anatomical models.
garnica-bohorquez-2023.apa: Garnica-Bohórquez, I., Güiza-Argüello, V. R., & López-Gualdrón, C. I. (2023). Effect of sterilization on the dimensional and mechanical behavior of polylactic acid pieces produced by fused deposition modeling. *Polymers, 15*(15), Article 3317. https://doi.org/10.3390/polym15153317

kiel-2022.title: Bacterial biofilm formation on nano-copper added PLA suited for 3D printed face masks
summary: Compared a filament sold as germ-killing (it contains copper) against regular PLA.
Grew 3 common hospital bacteria on both and counted what survived.
Bacteria stuck to and grew on every material tested, including the "germ-killing" filament.
The copper strongly slowed only 1 of the 3 bacteria.
Suggests that filaments sold as antibacterial may not protect against much.
kiel-2022.apa: Kiel, A., Kaltschmidt, B. P., Asghari, E., Hütten, A., Kaltschmidt, B., & Kaltschmidt, C. (2022). Bacterial biofilm formation on nano-copper added PLA suited for 3D printed face masks. *Microorganisms, 10*(2), Article 439. https://doi.org/10.3390/microorganisms10020439

rynio-2022.title: Effects of sterilization methods on different 3D printable materials for templates of physician-modified aortic stent grafts used in vascular surgery: A preliminary study
summary: Printed the same surgical template in 6 plastics, PLA included.
Deliberately contaminated them with bacteria, then tried several ways of killing the germs.
Every method eliminated the microorganisms. The type of plastic didn't matter for that.
The shape was the problem: steam at 121 °C badly deformed PLA, along with PETG and PP.
Shows that the type of plastic decides whether a tool survives the heat.
rynio-2022.apa: Rynio, P., Galant, K., Wójcik, Ł., Grygorcewicz, B., Kazimierczak, A., Falkowski, A., Gutowski, P., Dołęgowska, B., & Kawa, M. (2022). Effects of sterilization methods on different 3D printable materials for templates of physician-modified aortic stent grafts used in vascular surgery: A preliminary study. *International Journal of Molecular Sciences, 23*(7), Article 3539. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms23073539

fleischer-2020.title: The effect of chemical cleaning on mechanical properties of three-dimensional printed polylactic acid
summary: Tested whether repeated chemical cleaning weakens 3D-printed PLA, aimed at hospitals in low- and middle-income countries.
Printed pulling-test samples at 6 different printer settings, then soaked them in Cidex OPA or a chlorine solution.
Used 2 exposure patterns: 7 days straight, or 25 short cycles.
Weighed every sample before and after, then pulled them apart. A third of the treatments gained weight, up to 8.3%, but the samples with the smoothest surfaces did not change.
Strength moved in both directions: a median increase of 12.5%, and a largest decrease of 8.8%.
Warns that surface pores must be kept small so soaked-in disinfectant does not transfer to people.
fleischer-2020.apa: Fleischer, J. C., Diehl, J. C., Wauben, L. S. G. L., & Dankelman, J. (2020). The effect of chemical cleaning on mechanical properties of three-dimensional printed polylactic acid. *Journal of Medical Devices, 14*(1), Article 011109. https://doi.org/10.1115/1.4046120

vankova-2020.title: Polylactic acid as a suitable material for 3D printing of protective masks in times of COVID-19 pandemic
summary: Checked whether 3D-printed PLA can be cleaned and reused, and whether the plastic survives the cleaning.
Contaminated 1 cm squares of printed PLA with E. coli, a skin bacterium, and a yeast, then soaked them for 15 minutes in 96% ethanol, 70% isopropanol, or a bleach-type disinfectant.
All 3 disinfectants removed the bacteria and the yeast.
Five 15-minute rounds of isopropanol narrowed the gaps between printed lines from about 6 micrometers to 3.3–4, without major surface changes.
Also tested masks that volunteers actually wore for 4 hours.
Microscope images showed the pores were closed deeper inside the part, and no test particles passed through.
vankova-2020.apa: Vaňková, E., Kašparová, P., Khun, J., Machková, A., Julák, J., Sláma, M., Hodek, J., Ulrychová, L., Weber, J., Obrová, K., Kosulin, K., Lion, T., & Scholtz, V. (2020). Polylactic acid as a suitable material for 3D printing of protective masks in times of COVID-19 pandemic. *PeerJ, 8*, Article e10259. https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.10259

labakoum-2024.title: Effects of autoclaving and disinfection on 3D surgical guides using LCD technology for dental implant
summary: Compared 3 ways of treating 3D-printed dental surgical guides: autoclave at 121 °C, autoclave at 134 °C, and 20 minutes in 70% isopropyl alcohol.
Made 100 samples in total, with an untreated control group for comparison.
Used a 3-point bending test following ASTM D790, the standard for bending strength of plastic bars.
Both autoclave temperatures changed the shape and the mechanical behavior of the guides.
The alcohol group came out closest to the untreated control, so the authors recommended alcohol over heat.
Important limit: these were resin parts printed on an LCD printer, not PLA on a filament printer.
labakoum-2024.apa: Labakoum, B., Farhan, A., Ben Taleb, L., Mouhsen, A., & Lyazidi, A. (2024). Effects of autoclaving and disinfection on 3D surgical guides using LCD technology for dental implant. *3D Printing in Medicine, 10*, Article 14. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41205-024-00214-1

kaptan-2025.title: Investigation of the effect of exposure to liquid chemicals on the strength performance of 3D-printed parts from different filament types
summary: Soaked test bars of 8 different filament plastics in seven chemical agents, with isopropyl alcohol at both 75% and 99%, then pulled and struck them to see what strength was left.
Followed ASTM D638 for pulling and ASTM D256 for impact, with 3 samples per combination.
Samples were fully submerged for 1 hour, 24 hours, or 7 days, which is harsher than wiping a tool and letting it dry.
kaptan-2025.apa: Kaptan, A. (2025). Investigation of the effect of exposure to liquid chemicals on the strength performance of 3D-printed parts from different filament types. *Polymers, 17*(12), Article 1637. https://doi.org/10.3390/polym17121637

mai-2020.title: Antibacterial drug-release polydimethylsiloxane coating for 3D-printing dental polymer: Surface alterations and antimicrobial effects
summary: Explains why 3D-printed plastic holds onto bacteria: tiny pores form when air gets trapped between layers or when layers do not fuse completely.
Coated half of 60 printed disks with a silicone-based layer carrying an antiseptic, and left the other half bare.
The coating reduced surface irregularity and made the surface more water repelling.
Bacteria counts were significantly lower on the coated disks.
The study did not test the mechanical properties of the coating itself.
Limits: dental resin printing rather than PLA, and the coating released an antiseptic drug rather than acting as a plain sealant.
mai-2020.apa: Mai, H.-N., Hyun, D. C., Park, J. H., Kim, D.-Y., Lee, S. M., & Lee, D.-H. (2020). Antibacterial drug-release polydimethylsiloxane coating for 3D-printing dental polymer: Surface alterations and antimicrobial effects. *Pharmaceuticals, 13*(10), Article 304. https://doi.org/10.3390/ph13100304

tymrak-2014.title: Mechanical properties of components fabricated with open-source 3-D printers under realistic environmental conditions
summary: Measured the strength of parts from hobby printers in ordinary conditions, to show what a realistic scenario looks like.
Showed that hobby printers can produce results that can be reported and analyzed properly.
tymrak-2014.apa: Tymrak, B. M., Kreiger, M., & Pearce, J. M. (2014). Mechanical properties of components fabricated with open-source 3-D printers under realistic environmental conditions. *Materials & Design, 58*, 242–246. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2014.02.038

herigstad-2001.title: How to optimize the drop plate method for enumerating bacteria
herigstad-2001.note: This study does not count bacteria. The source is here to explain that limit.
summary: A reference paper for counting live bacteria by dropping small measured volumes onto agar plates.
Drop plating takes less time and effort than spreading the same sample across a plate, and the colonies can be counted faster.
There is no single standard way to do the method.
Works out how starting volume, dilution, and drop size affect the error in the count.
herigstad-2001.apa: Herigstad, B., Hamilton, M., & Heersink, J. (2001). How to optimize the drop plate method for enumerating bacteria. *Journal of Microbiological Methods, 44*(2), 121–129. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0167-7012(00)00241-4

cdc-2024.title: Guideline for disinfection and sterilization in healthcare facilities, 2008
summary: A guideline published by the CDC that sets out what level of cleaning a medical device needs in healthcare facilities.
Tools that enter normally germ-free body tissue need the highest level of treatment.
Steam is the preferred method for that highest level.
Cleaning comes first, because germ-killing steps fail if organic material is still on the surface of a tool.
cdc-2024.apa: Rutala, W. A., Weber, D. J., & Healthcare Infection Control Practices Advisory Committee. (2008). *Guideline for disinfection and sterilization in healthcare facilities, 2008*. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. https://www.cdc.gov/infection-control/hcp/disinfection-and-sterilization/index.html

cnc-kitchen-2018.title: TESTING 3D printed INFILL PATTERNS for their STRENGTH
summary: A YouTuber crushed small printed cubes to compare infill patterns on a modified tensile machine.
Every cube used identical walls, so the only thing that changed was the infill pattern.
He weighed a test batch first and adjusted the infill percentages so all samples used the same amount of plastic.
Cubes were weaker when crushed from the side than in the direction they were printed.
Some patterns went past the machine's limit, so they could not be measured accurately.
cnc-kitchen-2018.apa: CNC Kitchen. (2018, July 27). *TESTING 3D printed INFILL PATTERNS for their STRENGTH* [Video]. YouTube. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=upELI0HmzHc

bio-rad-laboratories-2012.title: Serial dilution and plate counts
bio-rad-laboratories-2012.note: This study does not count bacteria. The source is here to explain that limit.
summary: Shows how to dilute a bacterial culture step by step across a row of tubes.
Mixes each tube by vortexing and pipetting up and down between steps.
Spreads each dilution across the whole surface of an agar plate.
The plates are then stacked upside down and incubated before counting.
bio-rad-laboratories-2012.apa: Bio-Rad Laboratories. (2012, October 16). *Serial dilution and plate counts* [Video]. YouTube. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pmRUBYlPMBM

zhang-2023.title: Low cost universal tensile testing machine
summary: Describes a tensile tester of about $300, built from printed and common store-bought parts, as an alternative to commercial machines that start at $12,900.
It handles loads under 1000 N and can run compression tests as well as tension.
Argues that rapid-prototyping work doesn't always need the precision of a commercial machine.
zhang-2023.apa: Zhang, X. (2023, July 31). *Low cost universal tensile testing machine*. Hackaday.io. https://hackaday.io/project/192166-low-cost-universal-tensile-testing-machine

ozer-2025.title: Infiltration-assisted mechanical strengthening of 3D-printed polypropylene lattice and thin-walled tube structures
summary: A method for pushing epoxy into the hidden gaps inside a 3D print instead of only painting the outside.
Dipped printed parts into epoxy with help from an ultrasonic bath, at 4 different epoxy thicknesses (viscosities).
The epoxy reduced micro-voids and surface irregularities.
Weighed parts before and after, and used the weight gain to estimate how much of the inside got filled.
Thick epoxy mostly stayed on the outside as a shell, thin epoxy soaked in but left almost no surface layer, and medium thickness was the balance.
Shows that weight gain alone can be misleading, because it does not say whether the epoxy went inside or just built up on the surface.
Limits: tested on polypropylene rather than PLA, and aimed at crash strength rather than cleaning.
ozer-2025.apa: Özer, H. (2025). Infiltration-assisted mechanical strengthening of 3D-printed polypropylene lattice and thin-walled tube structures. *Polymers, 17*(19), Article 2604. https://doi.org/10.3390/polym17192604

crawford-2018.title: Reuse of catheters and devices labelled for single use: Evidence, recommendations and oversight
summary: Argues that reusing single-use devices can be ethically justified when it improves access for the least advantaged patients.
Safe reuse gives patients who can't afford the highest quality care a real chance at some level of care.
Sets conditions: reuse must be transparent, patients should be able to opt out, and devices must be expected to work about as well as new ones.
Says most of the safety studies behind reuse are from the 1980s and 1990s and vary in quality.
crawford-2018.apa: Crawford, T. C., & Eagle, K. A. (2018). Reuse of catheters and devices labelled for single use: Evidence, recommendations and oversight. *Heart Asia, 10*(2), Article e011033. https://doi.org/10.1136/heartasia-2018-011033

duffa-2025.title: Evaluating the efficacy of reprocessing contaminated single use devices for re-use in intensive care unit in Ethiopia
summary: Single-use devices may be routinely reprocessed and reused in low-income settings.
There was no standard protocol for reprocessing these devices, so the authors wrote one and tested it.
They swabbed used devices before and after reprocessing and counted the bacteria on each.
Bacteria were measured with colony counts (CFU) on real hospital equipment.
duffa-2025.apa: Duffa, Y. M., Kasa, Z. S., Aklilu, K. K., Senbato, F. R., Bonger, Z. T., Seyoum, E. T., Zeleke, E. D., Chekol, L. T., Mekuria, Z., Welelaw, S. M., Balada-Llasat, J.-M., Wang, S.-H., & Eguale, T. (2026). Evaluating the efficacy of reprocessing contaminated single use devices for re-use in intensive care unit in Ethiopia. *Antimicrobial Resistance & Infection Control, 15*, Article 14. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13756-025-01683-7

pepin-2014.title: Evolution of the global burden of viral infections from unsafe medical injections, 2000–2010
summary: Tracks how many viral infections worldwide come from unsafe medical injections, like reused injection equipment.

The World Health Organization's estimate for 2000 blamed unsafe injections for 5% of new HIV infections, 32% of new hepatitis B infections, and 40% of new hepatitis C infections in developing and transitional countries.
The estimates multiply how often equipment is reused, how common the virus already is, how likely it is to be passed on, and how many injections people get.
Shows what happens when reuse is caused by scarcity instead of choice.
pepin-2014.apa: Pépin, J., Abou Chakra, C. N., Pépin, E., Nault, V., & Valiquette, L. (2014). Evolution of the global burden of viral infections from unsafe medical injections, 2000–2010. *PLOS ONE, 9*(6), Article e99677. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0099677

akpa-inyang-2025.title: Ethical and regulatory issues in the application of 3D printing in orthopaedics: A scoping review
summary: When a hospital prints its own devices, it may become a de facto manufacturer.
This raises questions about who is responsible for quality and safety.
The rules for printing at the point of care are still undefined.
Printing facilities are expected to follow quality standards, which puts another burden on hospitals that print.
akpa-inyang-2025.apa: Akpa-Inyang, F., Rocher, A., O'Connor, M., & Marais, L. (2025). Ethical and regulatory issues in the application of 3D printing in orthopaedics: A scoping review. *Journal of Orthopaedic Reports, 4*(2, Suppl.), Article 100610. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jorep.2025.100610

ante-2023.title: Legal issues and underexplored data protection in medical 3D printing: A scoping review
summary: Reviewed 49 articles on the legal problems of 3D-printed medical devices.
Found that liability is an open issue when a personalized printed device fails.
The law doesn't cleanly separate custom-made devices from patient-matched ones.
The legal status of design (CAD) files is unclear, so it is not clear who owns a file or who is to blame if a device fails.
ante-2023.apa: Pettersson, A. B. V., Ballardini, R. M., Mimler, M., Li, P., Salmi, M., Minssen, T., Gibson, I., & Mäkitie, A. (2023). Legal issues and underexplored data protection in medical 3D printing: A scoping review. *Frontiers in Bioengineering and Biotechnology, 11*, Article 1102780. https://doi.org/10.3389/fbioe.2023.1102780

lantada-2023.title: Ethical issues of 4D printed medical devices
summary: Normally the manufacturer is accountable when a medical device injures someone.
That chain of responsibility breaks down when designs are shared online and can be printed anywhere.
Asks who answers for a design that someone downloaded and then modified: the original creator or the modifier.
Argues that regulators need ways to track design changes and control quality.
lantada-2023.apa: Díaz Lantada, A. (2023, June 8). Ethical issues of 4D printed medical devices. *IEEE Pulse*. https://www.embs.org/pulse/articles/ethical-issues-of-4d-printed-medical-devices/

elliott-2020.title: Engineers 3D-print patented valves for free to save coronavirus patients in Italy
summary: A hospital in Brescia, Italy ran short of ventilator valves during the 2020 COVID crisis.
The original valves reportedly cost thousands each (the exact price is disputed) and had to be swapped every 8 hours.
A local startup reverse-engineered the valve and printed about 100 for free, at about 1 euro of material each.
The founder said they had no intent to profit from or keep the design.
elliott-2020.apa: Elliott, J. K. (2020, March 18). Engineers 3D-print patented valves for free to save coronavirus patients in Italy. *Global News*. https://globalnews.ca/news/6695286/coronavirus-italy-3d-print-valves/

kent-2020.title: Covid-19: Start-up that saved lives with 3D-printed valve may face legal action
summary: Focuses on the legal threat around the printed valves instead of the rescue itself.
The original manufacturer allegedly declined to share blueprints and threatened to sue for patent infringement.
The valves were printed on site at the hospital with a filament printer.
Shows the 2 sides of the conflict: patients in need on one side, and patent holders on the other.
kent-2020.apa: Kent, C. (2020, March 18). Covid-19: Start-up that saved lives with 3D-printed valve may face legal action. *Medical Device Network*. https://www.medicaldevice-network.com/news/3d-printed-valves-covid-19-italy/

britton-2018.title: Is 3D printing a humanitarian technology?
summary: Describes an aid organization testing whether 3D printing medical supplies on site is worth doing in Nepal.
Targeted cheap but important items like umbilical cord clamps and oxygen supply fittings.
Argues the value of printing is after a disaster, when supply routes are broken.
The team ran 11 needs-assessment visits to hospitals and health posts before investing in any equipment.
Puts the focus on finding what people lack before deciding that 3D printing is the answer.
britton-2018.apa: Britton, B. (2018, May 9). Is 3D printing a humanitarian technology? *Frontier Tech Hub*. https://medium.com/frontier-technologies-hub/is-3d-printing-a-humanitarian-technology-e25222d81496

added.title: Effects of surface treatments on ABS mechanical properties from fused filament fabrication
summary: Brushed Smooth-On XTC-3D, the epoxy selected for this study, onto printed ABS.
Found lower moisture uptake, and tensile strength that was not significantly different.
The coating likely began separating from the plastic at a relatively low strain.
Limits: tested on ABS rather than PLA, and not through repeated disinfection.

added.title: Chemical disinfectants
summary: Says alcohol kills bacteria best as a 60% to 90% solution in water.
Says alcohol is not recommended for the highest level of germ-killing on surgical materials, mainly because it does not destroy bacterial spores.
Warns that alcohol can swell and harden rubber and certain plastic tubing after prolonged and repeated use.
